title: If one microservice is down, how do you handle it gracefully (circuit breaker, fallback, retry with backoff, timeout, bulkhead, graceful degradation, monitoring)?
shortTitle: If one microservice is down, how do you handle it gracefully

s1_definition.profdef: Graceful handling of a downstream failure is the practice of containing the blast radius of a failed dependency so the caller stays responsive instead of hanging or cascading the failure. The core patterns are timeouts (never wait forever), retries with backoff (give transient failures a second chance without stampeding), circuit breakers (stop calling a service that is clearly down), fallbacks (serve a degraded but useful response), bulkheads (isolate resources so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all threads), and monitoring (detect and alert on the failure). Together these turn a hard failure into graceful degradation.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India's branch depends on a central credit-score office to approve loans. One day the credit office phone line is dead. A graceful teller does not keep Rajesh waiting at the counter forever (that is a timeout), does not redial frantically hundreds of times (that is retry with backoff), and after noticing the line has been dead for a while, stops dialing altogether for a few minutes to save effort (that is a circuit breaker). Instead the teller tells Rajesh "we will give you a provisional decision based on your existing relationship" (that is a fallback and graceful degradation) and quietly files a report so the manager knows the line is down (that is monitoring). The customer still leaves served, and one broken phone line does not freeze the whole branch.
s1_definition.oneliner: When a dependency is down, fail fast with a timeout, retry transient errors with backoff, trip a circuit breaker to stop the bleeding, and serve a fallback so the user still gets a useful answer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Graceful handling of a downstream failure is the practice of containing the blast radius of a failed dependency so the caller stays responsive instead of hanging or cascading the failure. The core patterns are timeouts (never wait forever), retries with backoff (give transient failures a second chance without stampeding), circuit breakers (stop calling a service that is clearly down), fallbacks (serve a degraded but useful response), bulkheads (isolate resources so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all threads), and monitoring (detect and alert on the failure). Together these turn a hard failure into graceful degradation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India's branch depends on a central credit-score office to approve loans. One day the credit office phone line is dead. A graceful teller does not keep Rajesh waiting at the counter forever (that is a timeout), does not redial frantically hundreds of times (that is retry with backoff), and after noticing the line has been dead for a while, stops dialing altogether for a few minutes to save effort (that is a circuit breaker). Instead the teller tells Rajesh "we will give you a provisional decision based on your existing relationship" (that is a fallback and graceful degradation) and quietly files a report so the manager knows the line is down (that is monitoring). The customer still leaves served, and one broken phone line does not freeze the whole branch.

**One line to remember:** When a dependency is down, fail fast with a timeout, retry transient errors with backoff, trip a circuit breaker to stop the bleeding, and serve a fallback so the user still gets a useful answer.

sections.s2_technical:
A timeout is the first and most important defense. Every remote call must have a bounded wait, because the worst failure is not an error, it is a call that hangs forever and ties up a thread. In Resilience4j you configure a `TimeLimiter`, and with a WebClient you set a response timeout. For example, a payment call that normally returns in fifty milliseconds should time out at, say, two seconds, so a stuck instance releases the caller quickly.

Retry with backoff gives transient failures a second chance without creating a thundering herd. If a call fails, you wait a short, growing delay (exponential backoff) with a little randomness (jitter) and try again a limited number of times. The key rule is to only retry idempotent operations; retrying a non-idempotent transfer could double-charge Rajesh. For example, Resilience4j `@Retry(name = "paymentRetry")` with a configured `wait-duration` and `exponential-backoff-multiplier` handles this.

A circuit breaker stops calling a service that is clearly down. It watches the recent failure rate, and when failures cross a threshold it opens, meaning subsequent calls fail instantly without even attempting the network, which protects both the caller (no wasted threads) and the callee (no pile-on while it recovers). After a cooldown it goes half-open, letting a few trial calls through; if they succeed it closes again, if they fail it reopens. In Resilience4j you annotate with `@CircuitBreaker(name = "paymentCb", fallbackMethod = "fallback")`.

A fallback is the graceful answer when the primary path fails. It might return a cached value, a sensible default, or a queued-for-later acknowledgment. For example, if the fraud-scoring service is down, the fallback might apply a conservative default risk score and flag the transaction for later review, so the transfer is not simply refused.

A bulkhead isolates resources so one sick dependency cannot sink the whole ship. Named after the watertight compartments in a ship's hull, it limits how many concurrent calls or threads a given dependency may consume. If the statement-generation service becomes slow, a bulkhead caps it at, say, ten concurrent calls, so the remaining threads stay free to serve transfers. Resilience4j offers `@Bulkhead` with a `max-concurrent-calls` limit.

Graceful degradation is the overall philosophy: the system continues to provide core value with reduced functionality rather than failing completely. If notifications are down, the transfer still completes and the SMS is queued. Finally, monitoring and alerting tie it together: circuit breaker state changes, retry counts, timeout rates, and fallback invocations should emit metrics to Prometheus and alerts to the on-call engineer, because a silent fallback that masks an outage for days is its own kind of failure.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the transfer service calls a downstream fraud-check service before completing any transfer. One afternoon the fraud-check service crashed.

Problem 1 — the fraud call had no timeout, so every transfer thread blocked waiting for a reply that never came. Within minutes all the transfer service threads were stuck, and even simple balance checks stopped working. This is exactly what a timeout prevents: a bounded wait releases the thread fast so one dead dependency cannot freeze unrelated work.

Problem 2 — a naive fix added infinite retries, which hammered the already-struggling fraud service and delayed its recovery. This is exactly what retry with backoff and a circuit breaker fix: retries are limited and spaced out, and once failures are obviously sustained the breaker opens and stops calling entirely for a cooldown.

Problem 3 — simply rejecting every transfer while fraud-check was down would block legitimate customers like Rajesh. This is exactly what a fallback and graceful degradation provide: for low-value transfers we apply a conservative default score and flag the transaction for later manual review, so core banking keeps working.

The mini-project builds a `FraudCheckClient` that simulates a downstream call with a timeout. It builds a `ResilientTransferService` that wraps the fraud call with retry, circuit breaker, and a fallback. It builds the familiar `Account` with debit and credit. The demo runs transfers while the fraud service is healthy, then flips it to "down," and shows the breaker opening, the fallback serving provisional approvals, and monitoring counters updating.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, balance one million) transferring fifty thousand to Priya (CUR3001, balance two hundred fifty thousand), with the fraud-check service first healthy, then down.

Step 1: While healthy, the transfer service calls `checkFraudResilient`. The circuit breaker is CLOSED and allows the request. The fraud client returns a low score of ten. The breaker records success, the service debits Rajesh and credits Priya, and the transfer completes with risk ten.

Step 2: The fraud-check service is flipped down. The next transfer calls the client, which throws. The breaker records a failure and the retry loop waits two hundred milliseconds, then four hundred, trying up to three times.

Step 3: After three consecutive failures the breaker crosses its threshold and opens. It logs that it is now failing fast. The current call falls through to the fallback, which returns a conservative provisional score of thirty and increments the fallback counter.

Step 4: Subsequent transfers find the breaker OPEN. `allowRequest` returns false immediately, so no network call is attempted at all. Each goes straight to the fallback, keeping the thread free and not hammering the sick service.

Step 5: The fallback provisional score of thirty is below the block threshold, so the transfers still complete, Rajesh is debited, Priya is credited, and each transaction is flagged for later manual review. Core banking keeps working.

Step 6: Monitoring output shows the breaker is OPEN and the fallback was invoked several times, which is exactly the signal the on-call engineer needs to investigate the fraud service.

```
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    TRANSFER 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 SUCCESS (risk=10)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  Fraud-check service is now DOWN
2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  FRAUD-CHECK call failed for SAV2001 (service down)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  CIRCUIT open: stop calling dependency (failures=3)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 WARNING FALLBACK provisional risk=30 for SAV2001 (flagged for manual review)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    TRANSFER 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 SUCCESS (risk=30)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    Breaker state=OPEN, fallback invocations=5
```

                             └──────────────────────┘

  [CLOSED] ──failures >= threshold──→ [OPEN] ──cooldown elapsed──→ [HALF_OPEN]
     ▲                                                                 │
     │                                   trial success                 │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ┘
                                         trial failure → back to [OPEN]

  ── Call Chain (dependency DOWN) ───────────────────────────────

  1. transfer(rajesh, priya, 50000)
  2.   → checkFraudResilient("SAV2001", 50000)
  3.     → breaker.allowRequest() == true (CLOSED)
  4.     → fraudClient.score() throws  → breaker.onFailure()
  5.     → retry backoff 200ms, 400ms ... 3 failures
  6.     → breaker.onFailure() → state OPEN
  7.     → fallbackScore() → provisional 30, fallbackCount++

    Pre:  breaker initialized
    Post: always returns a usable score (real or fallback)
    Never: blocks longer than timeout × attempts; never throws upward

sections.s6_takeaway:
When one microservice is down, the goal is to contain the blast radius so the caller stays responsive and the failure does not cascade. I handle this with a layered set of resilience patterns, and I can speak to each one from real banking work. The first and most important is a timeout on every remote call, because the worst failure is not an error, it is a call that hangs forever and ties up threads. In our transfer service a fraud-check call that normally returns in fifty milliseconds times out at two seconds, so a stuck instance releases the thread quickly.

On top of timeouts I use retry with exponential backoff and jitter, but only for idempotent operations, because retrying a non-idempotent transfer could double-charge the customer. Retries give transient blips a second chance without creating a thundering herd. Then I wrap the call in a circuit breaker. It watches the recent failure rate, and once failures are clearly sustained it opens, so subsequent calls fail instantly without even touching the network. That protects my own threads and also protects the struggling dependency from a pile-on while it recovers. After a cooldown it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through before deciding to close again or reopen.

The piece that keeps customers served is the fallback, which is graceful degradation in action. When our fraud-check service went down, instead of rejecting every transfer, the fallback applied a conservative default risk score for low-value transfers and flagged them for later manual review, so legitimate customers like Rajesh were still served while high-risk cases stayed protected. I also use bulkheads, which cap how many concurrent calls a single dependency can consume, so if statement generation becomes slow it cannot starve the threads that handle transfers.

Finally, none of this is complete without monitoring and alerting. Circuit breaker state changes, retry counts, timeout rates, and fallback invocations all emit metrics to Prometheus, and we alert the on-call engineer when the breaker opens or the fallback rate spikes, because a silent fallback that quietly masks an outage for days is its own failure. In my projects we expose all of this through Resilience4j annotations and Spring Boot Actuator so it is declarative and observable.

The way I summarize it to an interviewer is this: fail fast with timeouts, retry transient errors with backoff, trip a circuit breaker to stop the bleeding, serve a fallback so the user still gets a useful answer, isolate with bulkheads, and watch everything with metrics and alerts. That turns one service being down from an outage into a brief, visible, graceful degradation.
